steps.title: Key Point
steps.body: Your vocabulary choices directly affect your AO6 mark (up to 16 marks). A wide, ambitious vocabulary demonstrates control and precision - but only when used appropriately.

steps.title: Connotation Matters
steps.body: "Cheap" and "inexpensive" have similar meanings but different connotations. "Cheap" suggests poor quality; "inexpensive" suggests good value. Choose the word with the right emotional shade.

steps.title: Common Repeat Offenders
steps.body: said, went, looked, got, nice, good, thing, something, very, really

steps.title: Warning
steps.body: Don't use words you don't fully understand. Misused ambitious vocabulary is worse than correctly used simple vocabulary.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Replace "very happy" with a single, more precise word. | What is the difference in connotation between "cheap" and "inexpensive"? | Rewrite "She walked slowly across the room" using a powerful verb instead of walked + slowly.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Ecstatic, overjoyed, elated, jubilant, delighted (any of these or similar). | "Cheap" has negative connotations of poor quality. "Inexpensive" has neutral/positive connotations of good value. Same basic meaning, different emotional impact. | She crept/ambled/trudged/meandered/strolled across the room (any precise verb that shows slow movement).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Build vocabulary gradually - learn a few new words each week Practice using new words in sentences before the exam Read widely to absorb vocabulary naturally Check you understand a word's meaning AND connotations Don't force ambitious vocabulary - use it where it fits Proofread for repeated words and find alternatives Consider register - match formality to task and audience Focus on verbs - they drive your writing
